title: Hosea 7:1–7
context: The LORD longs to heal Israel, but every approach uncovers more iniquity in Ephraim and in Samaria, the capital (7:1). The people forget that the LORD remembers all their wickedness (7:2). Verses 3–7 portray a court in turmoil: officials please the king with wickedness and lies, princes grow sick with wine (“On the day of our king”), and conspirators burn “like an oven” through the night until their anger flares in the morning. The oven image is vivid but difficult in its details. “All their kings have fallen” (7:7) is often linked with the series of assassinations in the northern kingdom recorded in 2 Kings 15:8–30, a likely but not certain background. The adultery language of verse 4 describes covenant unfaithfulness and possibly moral disorder, and these notes keep it sober. The section closes with the LORD’s lament, “There is no one among them who calls to me.” Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as a portrait of a nation whose leaders consume one another while no one turns to the LORD, and both see the LORD’s desire to heal as genuine.

verses.text: When I would heal Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim is uncovered, also the wickedness of Samaria; for they commit falsehood, and the thief enters in, and the gang of robbers ravages outside.
verses.arminianNotes: “When I would heal Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim is uncovered.” Arminian readers hear the LORD’s real desire to heal meeting resistance: the very approach of healing exposes sin that the people will not abandon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s healing presence bringing hidden sin into the light, and they note how widespread it is: falsehood, theft, and robbery inside and outside. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking healing with the exposure of sin, and both note Samaria, the capital, alongside Ephraim, showing corruption at the center of power.

verses.text: They don’t consider in their hearts that I remember all their wickedness. Now their own deeds have engulfed them. They are before my face.
verses.arminianNotes: “They don’t consider in their hearts that I remember all their wickedness.” Arminian readers see willful forgetfulness of God’s knowledge: people act as though unseen, and “their own deeds have engulfed them,” surrounding them with the consequences of what they chose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that God’s memory of sin is complete and that judgment comes through the consequences of sin itself. Shared ground: both traditions affirm God’s full knowledge and the self-entangling nature of sin, and both read “They are before my face” as a statement of the people’s inescapable accountability before the LORD.

verses.text: They make the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies.
verses.arminianNotes: “They make the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies.” Arminian readers see a court that rewards flattery and deceit, where officials and rulers share in the corruption by their own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an inversion of royal justice: rather than restraining evil, the king delights in it (compare Proverbs 16:12; 20:8). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a portrait of corrupt leadership, and both treat the intrigue of verses 3–7 as likely tied to the unstable politics of the northern kingdom, though the specific events are not named.

verses.text: They are all adulterers. They are burning like an oven that the baker stops stirring, from the kneading of the dough, until it is leavened.
verses.arminianNotes: “They are all adulterers. They are burning like an oven that the baker stops stirring.” The oven pictures passion held back and ready to flare. Arminian readers see desire nursed and stoked until it bursts out, a sobering picture of how unchecked impulses grow when they are fed rather than resisted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heat as inner corruption waiting for its moment, like a baker’s fire left to build while the dough rises. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge that the details of the image are difficult, read “adulterers” as covenant unfaithfulness and possibly moral disorder as well, and keep the treatment sober.

verses.text: On the day of our king, the princes made themselves sick with the heat of wine. He joined his hand with mockers.
verses.arminianNotes: “On the day of our king, the princes made themselves sick with the heat of wine.” A royal celebration becomes a scene of drunkenness. Arminian readers see the king who “joined his hand with mockers” as complicit in the folly that will undo him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the day of festivity as the setting of conspiracy, with leaders dulled by wine while plotters prepare their moment. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as corruption at court, possibly the backdrop of a coup, and both hold any specific historical reference with caution, since the verse does not name the king.

verses.text: For they have prepared their heart like an oven, while they lie in wait. Their anger smolders all night. In the morning it burns as a flaming fire.
verses.arminianNotes: “For they have prepared their heart like an oven, while they lie in wait.” Arminian readers see deliberate scheming: anger is fed through the night and breaks out in the morning, and the plotters are responsible for the hearts they prepared.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heart as the source of action (compare Proverbs 4:23; Jeremiah 17:9), and the smoldering anger as revealing how sin hides and then erupts. Shared ground: both traditions read the oven as an image of premeditated conspiracy, and both agree that the evil described arises from within those who plot it.

verses.text: They are all hot as an oven, and devour their judges. All their kings have fallen. There is no one among them who calls to me.
verses.arminianNotes: “All their kings have fallen. There is no one among them who calls to me.” Many readers link the fallen kings with the assassinations recorded in 2 Kings 15:8–30. Arminian readers note the tragedy that in all the turmoil no one turns to the LORD, though he remained ready to hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the LORD’s verdict that no one calls on him, and see the fall of kings as God’s judgment working through human violence. Shared ground: both traditions treat the link to 2 Kings 15 as likely but not certain, and both see the absence of prayer amid crisis as the deepest symptom of Israel’s condition.
